section.heading: 8.6 Curves and Surfaces
section.paragraph: For thousands of years, builders used long thin strips of wood to create the hull of a boat. In more recent times, designers used long, flexible metal strips to lay out the surfaces of cars and airplanes. Weights and pegs shaped the strips into smooth curves called natural cubic splines. The curve between two successive control points (pegs or weights) has a parametric representation using cubic polynomials. Unfortunately, such curves have the property that moving one control point affects the shape of the entire curve, because of physical forces that the pegs and weights exert on the strip. Design engineers had long wanted local control of the curve—in which movement of one control point would affect only a small portion of the curve. In 1962, a French automotive engineer, Pierre Bézier, solved this problem by adding extra control points and using a class of curves now called by his name.
section.heading: Bézier Curves
section.paragraph: The curves described in this section play an important role in computer graphics as well as engineering. For example, they are used in Adobe Illustrator and Macromedia Freehand, and in application programming languages such as OpenGL. These curves permit a program to store exact information about curved segments and surfaces in a relatively small number of control points. All graphics commands for the segments and surfaces have only to be computed for the control points. The special structure of these curves also speeds up other calculations in the “graphics pipeline” that creates the final display on the viewing screen.

Exercises in Section 8.3 introduced quadratic Bézier curves and showed one method for constructing Bézier curves of higher degree. The discussion here focuses on quadratic and cubic Bézier curves, which are determined by three or four control points, denoted by $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . These points can be in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ or $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ , or they can be represented by homogeneous forms in $$\mathbb{R}^{3}$$ or $$\mathbb{R}^{4}$$ . The standard parametric descriptions of these curves, for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ , are
$$\mathbf{w} \left(\right. t \left.\right) & = & \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{2} \mathbf{p}_{0} + 2 t ( 1 - t ) \mathbf{p}_{1} + t^{2} \mathbf{p}_{2}$$

$$\mathbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) & = & \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{3} \mathbf{p}_{0} + 3 t \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{2} \mathbf{p}_{1} + 3 t^{2} ( 1 - t ) \mathbf{p}_{2} + t^{3} \mathbf{p}_{3}$$

Figure 1 shows two typical curves. Usually, the curves pass through only the initial and terminal control points, but a Bézier curve is always in the convex hull of its control points. (See Exercises 25–28 in Section 8.3.)

image.alt: Quadratic and cubic Bezier curves with three and four control points, respectively, are shown.

figure.caption: Figure 1 Quadratic and cubic Bézier curves

section.paragraph: Bézier curves are useful in computer graphics because their essential properties are preserved under the action of linear transformations and translations. For instance, if $$A$$ is a matrix of appropriate size, then from the linearity of matrix multiplication, for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ ,﻿

$$A \mathbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) & = & A \left[\right. \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{3} \mathbf{p}_{0} + 3 t \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{2} \mathbf{p}_{1} + 3 t^{2} ( 1 - t ) \mathbf{p}_{2} + t^{3} \mathbf{p}_{3} \left]\right. & = & \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{3} A \mathbf{p}_{0} + 3 t \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{2} A \mathbf{p}_{1} + 3 t^{2} ( 1 - t ) A \mathbf{p}_{2} + t^{3} A \mathbf{p}_{3}$$
The new control points are $$A\textbf{p}_{0},\ldots,A\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . Translations of Bézier curves are considered in Exercise 1.

The curves in Figure 1 suggest that the control points determine the tangent lines to the curves at the initial and terminal control points. Recall from calculus that for any parametric curve, say $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ , the direction of the tangent line to the curve at a point $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ is given by the derivative $$\mathbf{y}\prime(t)$$ , called the tangent vector of the curve. (This derivative is computed entry by entry.)

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Determine how the tangent vector of the quadratic Bézier curve $$\textbf{w}(t)$$ is related to the control points of the curve, at $$t = 0$$ and $$t = 1$$ .﻿
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: Write the weights in equation (1) as simple polynomials
$$\textbf{w} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \left(\right. 1 - 2 t + t^{2} \left.\right) \textbf{p}_{0} + \left(\right. 2 t - 2 t^{2} \left.\right) \textbf{p}_{1} + t^{2} \textbf{p}_{2}$$
Then, because differentiation is a linear transformation on functions,
$$\mathbf{w} ' ( t ) = ( - 2 + 2 t ) \textbf{p}_{0} + ( 2 - 4 t ) \textbf{p}_{1} + 2 t \textbf{p}_{2}$$
So

$$\mathbf{w} ' ( 0 \left.\right) & = - 2 \textbf{p}_{0} + 2 \textbf{p}_{1} = 2 ( \textbf{p}_{1} - \textbf{p}_{0} ) \mathbf{w} ' ( 1 \left.\right) & = - 2 \textbf{p}_{1} + 2 \textbf{p}_{2} = 2 ( \textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{p}_{1} )$$

The tangent vector at $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , for instance, points from $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , but it is twice as long as the segment from $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ . Notice that $$\mathbf{w}\prime(0) = \textbf{0}$$ when $$\textbf{p}_{1} = \textbf{p}_{0}$$ . In this case, $$\textbf{w}(t) = \left( 1 - t^{2} \right)\textbf{p}_{1} + t^{2}\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and the graph of $$\textbf{w}(t)$$ is the line segment from $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ .﻿

section.heading: Connecting Two Bézier Curves
section.paragraph: Two basic Bézier curves can be joined end to end, with the terminal point of the first curve $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ being the initial point $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ of the second curve $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ . The combined curve is said to have $$G^{0}$$ geometric continuity (at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ ) because the two segments join at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ . If the tangent line to curve $$1$$ at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ has a different direction than the tangent line to curve $$2$$ , then a “corner,” or abrupt change of direction, may be apparent at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ . See Figure 2.

image.alt: A figure shows G to the 0 continuity with four line segments in the form a step along with two Bezier curves.

section.paragraph: To avoid a sharp bend, it usually suffices to adjust the curves to have what is called $$G^{1}$$ geometric continuity, where both tangent vectors at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ point in the same direction. That is, the derivatives $$\mathbf{x}\prime(1)$$ and $$\mathbf{y}\prime(0)$$ point in the same direction, even though their magnitudes may be different. When the tangent vectors are actually equal at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , the tangent vector is continuous at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and the combined curve is said to have $$C^{1}$$ continuity, or $$C^{1}$$ parametric continuity. Figure 3 shows $$G^{1}$$ continuity in (a) and $$C^{1}$$ continuity in (b).

image.alt: A graph shows G to the continuity and C to the 1 continuity with four control points in the form of a rectangle with its bottom left open.

figure.caption: Figure 3 (a) G1 continuity and (b) C1 continuity

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ determine two quadratic Bézier curves, with control points $$\{\textbf{p}_{0},\textbf{p}_{1},\textbf{p}_{2}\}$$ and $$\left\{ \textbf{p}_{2},\textbf{p}_{3},\textbf{p}_{4} \right\}$$ , respectively. The curves are joined at $$\textbf{p}_{2} = \textbf{x}(1) = \textbf{y}(0)$$ .

list.item: Suppose the combined curve has $$G^{1}$$ continuity (at $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ ). What algebraic restriction does this condition impose on the control points? Express this restriction in geometric language.
Repeat part (a) for $$C^{1}$$ continuity.

example.heading: Solution

list.item: From Example 1, $$\mathbf{x}\prime(1) = 2(\textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{p}_{1})$$ . Also, using the control points for $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ in place of $$\textbf{w}(t)$$ , Example 1 shows that $$\mathbf{y}\prime(0) = 2(\textbf{p}_{3} - \textbf{p}_{2})$$ . $$G^{1}$$ continuity means that $$\mathbf{y}\prime(0) = k\mathbf{x}\prime(1)$$ for some positive constant $$k$$ . Equivalently,

example.paragraph: $$\mathbf{p}_{3} - \mathbf{p}_{2} = k ( \mathbf{p}_{2} - \mathbf{p}_{1} ) , \text{with} k > 0$$

list.item: Geometrically, (3) implies that $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ lies on the line segment from $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . To prove this, let $$t = (k + 1)^{- 1}$$ , and note that $$0 < t < 1$$ . Solve for $$k$$ to obtain $$k = (1 - t)/t$$ . When this expression is used for $$k$$ in (3), a rearrangement shows that $$\textbf{p}_{2} = (1 - t)\textbf{p}_{1} + t\textbf{p}_{3}$$ , which verifies the assertion about $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ .﻿

$$C^{1}$$ continuity means that $$\mathbf{y}\prime(0) = \mathbf{x}\prime(1)$$ . Thus $$2\left( \textbf{p}_{3} - \textbf{p}_{2} \right) = 2\left( \textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{p}_{1} \right)$$ , so $$\textbf{p}_{3} - \textbf{p}_{2} = \textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2} = \left( \textbf{p}_{1} + \textbf{p}_{3} \right)/2$$ . Geometrically, $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is the midpoint of the line segment from $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . See Figure 3.

section.paragraph: Figure 4 shows $$C^{1}$$ continuity for two cubic Bézier curves. Notice how the point joining the two segments lies in the middle of the line segment between the adjacent control points.

image.alt: A figure shows two cubic Bezier curves along a line segment and a tilted pentagon with its bottom left side missing.

section.paragraph: Two curves have $$C^{2}$$ (parametric) continuity when they have $$C^{1}$$ continuity and the second derivatives $$\mathbf{x}''(1)$$ and $$\mathbf{y}''(0)$$ are equal. This is possible for cubic Bézier curves, but it severely limits the positions of the control points. Another class of cubic curves, called $$B-splines$$ , always have $$C^{2}$$ continuity because each pair of curves share three control points rather than one. Graphics figures using $$\text{B-splines}$$ have more control points and consequently require more computations. Some exercises for this section examine these curves.

Surprisingly, if $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ join at $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ , the apparent smoothness of the curve at $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ is usually the same for both $$G^{1}$$ continuity and $$C^{1}$$ continuity. This is because the magnitude of $$\mathbf{x}\prime(t)$$ is not related to the physical shape of the curve. The magnitude reflects only the mathematical parameterization of the curve. For instance, if a new vector function $$\textbf{z}(t)$$ equals $$\textbf{x}(2t)$$ , then the point $$\textbf{z}(t)$$ traverses the curve from $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ twice as fast as the original version, because $$2t$$ reaches $$1$$ when $$t$$ is $$.5$$ . But, by the chain rule of calculus, $$\mathbf{z}\prime(t) = 2 \cdot \mathbf{x}\prime(2t)$$ , so the tangent vector to $$\textbf{z}(t)$$ at $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ is twice the tangent vector to $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ at $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ .﻿

In practice, many simple Bézier curves are joined to create graphics objects. Typesetting programs provide one important application, because many letters in a type font involve curved segments. Each letter in a PostScript® font, for example, is stored as a set of control points, along with information on how to construct the “outline” of the letter using line segments and Bézier curves. Enlarging such a letter basically requires multiplying the coordinates of each control point by one constant scale factor. Once the outline of the letter has been computed, the appropriate solid parts of the letter are filled in. Figure 5 illustrates this for a character in a PostScript font. Note the control points.

image.alt: Two figures show a PostScript character Q along with its control points given by line segments.

section.heading: Matrix Equations for Bézier Curves
section.paragraph: Since a Bézier curve is a linear combination of control points using polynomials as weights, the formula for $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ may be written as

$$\mathbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\mathbf{p}_{0} & \mathbf{p}_{1} & \mathbf{p}_{2} & \mathbf{p}_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{3} \\ 3 t \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{2} \\ 3 t^{2} \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) \\ t^{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\mathbf{p}_{0} & \mathbf{p}_{1} & \mathbf{p}_{2} & \mathbf{p}_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 - 3 t + 3 t^{2} - t^{3} \\ 3 t - 6 t^{2} + 3 t^{3} \\ 3 t^{2} - 3 t^{3} \\ t^{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\mathbf{p}_{0} & \mathbf{p}_{1} & \mathbf{p}_{2} & \mathbf{p}_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & - 3 & 3 & - 1 \\ 0 & 3 & - 6 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & - 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 \\ t \\ t^{2} \\ t^{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

The matrix whose columns are the four control points is called a geometry matrix, $$G$$ . The $$4 \times 4$$ matrix of polynomial coefficients is the Bézier basis matrix, $$M_{B}$$ . If $$\textbf{u}(t)$$ is the column vector of powers of $$t$$ , then the Bézier curve is given by
$$\textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = G M_{B} \textbf{u} \left(\right. t \left.\right)$$

Other parametric cubic curves in computer graphics are written in this form, too. For instance, if the entries in the matrix $$M_{B}$$ are changed appropriately, the resulting curves are $$\text{B-splines}$$ . They are “smoother” than Bézier curves, but they do not pass through any of the control points. A Hermite cubic curve arises when the matrix $$M_{B}$$ is replaced by a Hermite basis matrix. In this case, the columns of the geometry matrix consist of the starting and ending points of the curves and the tangent vectors to the curves at those points.1
The Bézier curve in equation (4) can also be “factored” in another way, to be used in the discussion of Bézier surfaces. For convenience later, the parameter $$t$$ is replaced by a parameter $$s$$ :

$$\mathbf{x} ( s ) & = & \mathbf{u} \left(( s )\right)^{T} M_{B}^{T} \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\mathbf{p}_{0} \\ \mathbf{p}_{1} \\ \mathbf{p}_{2} \\ \mathbf{p}_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. = \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & s & s^{2} & s^{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ - 3 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & - 6 & 3 & 0 \\ - 1 & 3 & - 3 & 1\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\mathbf{p}_{0} \\ \mathbf{p}_{1} \\ \mathbf{p}_{2} \\ \mathbf{p}_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & \left[\right. \left(( 1 - s )\right)^{3} 3 s \left(( 1 - s )\right)^{2} 3 s^{2} ( 1 - s ) s^{3} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\mathbf{p}_{0} \\ \mathbf{p}_{1} \\ \mathbf{p}_{2} \\ \mathbf{p}_{3}\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$

This formula is not quite the same as the transpose of the product on the right of (4), because $$\textbf{x}(s)$$ and the control points appear in (5) without transpose symbols. The matrix of control points in (5) is called a geometry vector. This should be viewed as a $$4 \times 1$$ block (partitioned) matrix whose entries are column vectors. The matrix to the left of the geometry vector, in the second part of (5), can be viewed as a block matrix, too, with a scalar in each block. The partitioned matrix multiplication makes sense, because each (vector) entry in the geometry vector can be left-multiplied by a scalar as well as by a matrix. Thus, the column vector $$\textbf{x}(s)$$ is represented by (5).
section.heading: Bézier Surfaces
section.paragraph: A $$3D$$ bicubic surface patch can be constructed from a set of four Bézier curves. Consider the four geometry matrices

$$\left[\right. \begin{matrix}p_{11} & p_{12} & p_{13} & p_{14}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}p_{21} & p_{22} & p_{23} & p_{24}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}p_{31} & p_{32} & p_{33} & p_{34}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}p_{41} & p_{42} & p_{43} & p_{44}\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
and recall from equation (4) that a Bézier curve is produced when any one of these matrices is multiplied on the right by the following vector of weights:

$$M_{B} u \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \left[\right. \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{3} 3 t \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{2} 3 t^{2} \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) t^{3} \left]\right.$$

Let $$G$$ be the block (partitioned) $$4 \times 4$$ matrix whose entries are the control points $$\textbf{p}_{ij}$$ displayed above. Then the following product is a block $$4 \times 1$$ matrix, and each entry is a Bézier curve:

$$G M_{B} u \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \left[\right. p _{11} & p_{12} & p_{13} & p_{14} p_{21} & p_{22} & p_{23} & p_{24} p_{31} & p_{32} & p_{33} & p_{34} p_{41} & p_{42} & p_{43} & p_{44} \left]\right. \left[\right. \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{3} 3 t \left(\left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right)\right)^{2} 3 t^{2} \left(\right. 1 - t \left.\right) t^{3} \left]\right.$$
In fact,

$$G M_{B} \textbf{u} ( t ) = \begin{bmatrix} \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{3} \textbf{p}_{11} + 3 t \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{2} \textbf{p}_{12} + 3 t^{2} ( 1 - t ) \textbf{p}_{13} + t^{3} \textbf{p}_{14} \\ \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{3} \textbf{p}_{21} + 3 t \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{2} \textbf{p}_{22} + 3 t^{2} ( 1 - t ) \textbf{p}_{23} + t^{3} \textbf{p}_{24} \\ \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{3} \textbf{p}_{31} + 3 t \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{2} \textbf{p}_{32} + 3 t^{2} ( 1 - t ) \textbf{p}_{33} + t^{3} \textbf{p}_{34} \\ \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{3} \textbf{p}_{41} + 3 t \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{2} \textbf{p}_{42} + 3 t^{2} ( 1 - t ) \textbf{p}_{43} + t^{3} \textbf{p}_{44} \end{bmatrix}$$

Now fix $$t$$ . Then $$GM_{B}\textbf{u}(t)$$ is a column vector that can be used as a geometry vector in equation (5) for a Bézier curve in another variable $$s$$ . This observation produces the Bézier bicubic surface:
$$\textbf{x} ( s , t ) = \textbf{u} \left(( s )\right)^{T} M_{B}^{T} G M_{B} \textbf{u} ( t ) , where 0 \leq s , t \leq 1$$

The formula for $$\textbf{x}(s,t)$$ is a linear combination of the sixteen control points. If one imagines that these control points are arranged in a fairly uniform rectangular array, as in Figure 6, then the Bézier surface is controlled by a web of eight Bézier curves, four in the “ $$s \text{-direction}$$ ” and four in the “ $$t \text{-direction}$$ .” The surface actually passes through the four control points at its “corners.” When it is in the middle of a larger surface, the sixteen-point surface shares its twelve boundary control points with its neighbors.

image.alt: A figure shows a Bezier bicubic surface patch with sixteen control points.

figure.caption: Figure 6 Sixteen control points for a Bézier bicubic surface patch

section.heading: Approximations to Curves and Surfaces
section.paragraph: In CAD programs and in programs used to create realistic computer games, the designer often works at a graphics workstation to compose a “scene” involving various geometric structures. This process requires interaction between the designer and the geometric objects. Each slight repositioning of an object requires new mathematical computations by the graphics program. Bézier curves and surfaces can be useful in this process because they involve fewer control points than objects approximated by many polygons. This dramatically reduces the computation time and speeds up the designer’s work.

After the scene composition, however, the final image preparation has different computational demands that are more easily met by objects consisting of flat surfaces and straight edges, such as polyhedra. The designer needs to render the scene, by introducing light sources, adding color and texture to surfaces, and simulating reflections from the surfaces.

Computing the direction of a reflected light at a point $$\textbf{p}$$ on a surface, for instance, requires knowing the directions of both the incoming light and the surface normal—the vector perpendicular to the tangent plane at $$\textbf{p}$$ . Computing such normal vectors is much easier on a surface composed of, say, tiny flat polygons than on a curved surface whose normal vector changes continuously as $$\textbf{p}$$ moves. If $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ are adjacent vertices of a flat polygon, then the surface normal is just plus or minus the cross product $$\left( \textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{p}_{1} \right) \times \left( \textbf{p}_{2} - \textbf{p}_{3} \right)$$ . When the polygon is small, only one normal vector is needed for rendering the entire polygon. Also, two widely used shading routines, Gouraud shading and Phong shading, both require a surface to be defined by polygons.

As a result of these needs for flat surfaces, the Bézier curves and surfaces from the scene composition stage now are usually approximated by straight line segments and polyhedral surfaces. The basic idea for approximating a Bézier curve or surface is to divide the curve or surface into smaller pieces, with more and more control points.
section.heading: Recursive Subdivision of Bézier Curves and Surfaces
section.paragraph: Figure 7 shows the four control points $$\textbf{p}_{0},\ldots,\textbf{p}_{3}$$ for a Bézier curve, along with control points for two new curves, each coinciding with half of the original curve. The “left” curve begins at $$\textbf{q}_{0} = \textbf{p}_{0}$$ and ends at $$\textbf{q}_{3}$$ , at the midpoint of the original curve. The “right” curve begins at $$\textbf{r}_{0} = \textbf{q}_{3}$$ and ends at $$\textbf{r}_{3} = \textbf{p}_{3}$$ .﻿

image.alt: A figure shows the Bezier curve along with its subdivision inside an isosceles trapezium that is left open at the bottom.

figure.caption: Figure 7 Subdivision of a Bézier curve

section.paragraph: Figure 8 shows how the new control points enclose regions that are “thinner” than the region enclosed by the original control points. As the distances between the control points decrease, the control points of each curve segment also move closer to a line segment. This variation-diminishing property of Bézier curves depends on the fact that a Bézier curve always lies in the convex hull of the control points.

image.alt: A figure shows the convex hulls of the control points with a Bezier curve, a subdivision of the Bezier curve, and a triangle intersecting at a point inside an isosceles trapezium.

figure.caption: Figure 8 Convex hulls of the control points

section.paragraph: The new control points are related to the original control points by simple formulas. Of course, $$\textbf{q}_{0} = \textbf{p}_{0}$$ and $$\textbf{r}_{3} = \textbf{p}_{3}$$ . The midpoint of the original curve $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ occurs at $$\textbf{x}(.5)$$ when $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ has the standard parameterization,

$$\textbf{x} \left(\right. t \left.\right) = \left(\right. 1 - 3 t + 3 t^{2} - t^{3} \left.\right) \textbf{p}_{0} + \left(\right. 3 t - 6 t^{2} + 3 t^{3} \left.\right) \textbf{p}_{1} + \left(\right. 3 t^{2} - 3 t^{3} \left.\right) \textbf{p}_{2} + t^{3} \textbf{p}_{3}$$
for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ . Thus, the new control points $$\textbf{q}_{3}$$ and $$\textbf{r}_{0}$$ are given by
$$\textbf{q}_{3} = \textbf{r}_{0} = \textbf{x} ( .5 ) = \frac{1}{8} ( \textbf{p}_{0} + 3 \textbf{p}_{1} + 3 \textbf{p}_{2} + \textbf{p}_{3} )$$

The formulas for the remaining “interior” control points are also simple, but the derivation of the formulas requires some work involving the tangent vectors of the curves. By definition, the tangent vector to a parameterized curve $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ is the derivative $$\mathbf{x}\prime(t)$$ . This vector shows the direction of the line tangent to the curve at $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ . For the Bézier curve in (7),
for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ . In particular,
$$\mathbf{x} ' ( 0 ) = 3 ( \textbf{p}_{1} - \textbf{p}_{0} ) and \mathbf{x} ' ( 1 ) = 3 ( \textbf{p}_{3} - \textbf{p}_{2} )$$

Geometrically, $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ is on the line tangent to the curve at $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is on the line tangent to the curve at $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . See Figure 8. Also, from $$\textbf{x'}(t)$$ , compute
$$\mathbf{x} ' ( .5 ) = \frac{3}{4} ( - \textbf{p}_{0} - \textbf{p}_{1} + \textbf{p}_{2} + \textbf{p}_{3} )$$

Let $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ be the Bézier curve determined by $$\textbf{q}_{0},\ldots,\textbf{q}_{3}$$ , and let $$\textbf{z}(t)$$ be the Bézier curve determined by $$\textbf{r}_{0},\ldots,\textbf{r}_{3}$$ . Since $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ traverses the same path as $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ but only gets to $$\textbf{x}(.5)$$ as $$t$$ goes from $$0$$ to $$1$$ , $$\textbf{y}(t) = \textbf{x}(.5t)$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ . Similarly, since $$\textbf{z}(t)$$ starts at $$\textbf{x}(.5)$$ when $$t = 0$$ , $$\textbf{z}(t) = \textbf{x}(.5 + .5t)$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ . By the chain rule for derivatives,
$$\mathbf{y} ' ( t ) = .5 \mathbf{x} ' ( .5 t ) and \mathbf{z} ' ( t ) = . 5 \mathbf{x} ' ( .5 + .5 t ) \text{for} 0 \leq t \leq 1$$
From (9) with $$\mathbf{y}\prime(0)$$ in place of $$\mathbf{x}\prime(0)$$ , from (11) with $$t = 0$$ , and from (9), the control points for $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ satisfy
$$3 ( \textbf{q}_{1} - \textbf{q}_{0} ) = \mathbf{y} ' ( 0 ) = .5 \mathbf{x} ' ( 0 ) = \frac{3}{2} ( \textbf{p}_{1} - \textbf{p}_{0} )$$
From (9) with $$\mathbf{y}\prime(1)$$ in place of $$\mathbf{x}\prime(1)$$ , from (11) with $$t = 1$$ , and from (10),
$$3 ( \textbf{q}_{3} - \textbf{q}_{2} ) = \textbf{y}^{'} ( 1 ) = .5 \textbf{x}^{'} ( .5 ) = \frac{3}{8} ( - \textbf{p}_{0} - \textbf{p}_{1} + \textbf{p}_{2} + \textbf{p}_{3} )$$

Equations (8), (9), (10), (12), and (13) can be solved to produce the formulas for $$\textbf{q}_{0},\ldots,\textbf{q}_{3}$$ shown in Exercise 17. Geometrically, the formulas are displayed in Figure 9. The interior control points $$\textbf{q}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{r}_{2}$$ are the midpoints, respectively, of the segment from $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ and the segment from $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ . When the midpoint of the segment from $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ to $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ is connected to $$\textbf{q}_{1}$$ , the resulting line segment has $$\textbf{q}_{2}$$ in the middle!

image.alt: A figure shows the geometric structure of new control points with an isosceles trapezium.

figure.caption: Figure 9 Geometric structure of new control points

section.paragraph: This completes one step of the subdivision process. The “recursion” begins, and both new curves are subdivided. The recursion continues to a depth at which all curves are sufficiently straight. Alternatively, at each step the recursion can be “adaptive” and not subdivide one of the two new curves if that curve is sufficiently straight. Once the subdivision completely stops, the endpoints of each curve are joined by line segments, and the scene is ready for the next step in the final image preparation.

A Bézier bicubic surface has the same variation-diminishing property as the Bézier curves that make up each cross-section of the surface, so the process described above can be applied in each cross-section. With the details omitted, here is the basic strategy. Consider the four “parallel” Bézier curves whose parameter is $$s$$ , and apply the subdivision process to each of them. This produces four sets of eight control points; each set determines a curve as $$s$$ varies from $$0$$ to $$1$$ . As $$t$$ varies, however, there are eight curves, each with four control points. Apply the subdivision process to each of these sets of four points, creating a total of $$64$$ control points. Adaptive recursion is possible in this setting, too, but there are some subtleties involved.2

note.title: Practice Problems
note.heading: Practice Problems
note.paragraph: A spline usually refers to a curve that passes through specified points. A $$\text{B-spline}$$ , however, usually does not pass through its control points. A single segment has the parametric form

$$\mathbf{x} ( t ) = \frac{1}{6} \left[\right. \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{3} \mathbf{p}_{0} + ( 3 t^{3} - 6 t^{2} + 4 ) \mathbf{p}_{1} + \left(- \text{3} t^{3} + 3 t^{2} + 3 t + 1\right) \mathbf{p}_{2} + t^{3} \mathbf{p}_{3} \left]\right.$$

for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ , where $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ are the control points. When $$t$$ varies from $$0$$ to $$1$$ , $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ creates a short curve that lies close to $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{p}_{1}\textbf{p}_{2}}$$ . Basic algebra shows that the $$\text{B-spline}$$ formula can also be written as

$$\mathbf{x} ( t ) = \frac{1}{6} \left[\left(( 1 - t )\right)^{3} \mathbf{p}_{0} + ( 3 t \left(( 1 - t )\right)^{2} - 3 t + 4 ) \mathbf{p}_{1} + ( 3 t^{2} ( 1 - t ) + 3 t + 1 ) \mathbf{p}_{2} + t^{3} \mathbf{p}_{3}\right]$$

This shows the similarity with the Bézier curve. Except for the $$1/6$$ factor at the front, the $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ and $$\textbf{p}_{3}$$ terms are the same. The $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ component has been increased by $$- 3t + 4$$ and the $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ component has been increased by $$3t + 1$$ . These components move the curve closer to $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{p}_{1}\textbf{p}_{2}}$$ than the Bézier curve. The $$1/6$$ factor is necessary to keep the sum of the coefficients equal to $$1$$ . Figure 10 compares a $$\text{B-spline}$$ with a Bézier curve that has the same control points.

figure.caption: Figure 10 A B-spline segment and a Bézier curve

That is, show that $$\textbf{x}^{ \text{\prime\prime} }(1) = \textbf{y}^{ \text{\prime\prime} }(0)$$ . This higher-order continuity is desirable in CAD applications such as automotive body design, since the curves and surfaces appear much smoother. However, $$\text{B-spline}$$ require three times the computation of Bézier curves, for curves of comparable length. For surfaces, $$\text{B-spline}$$ require nine times the computation of Bézier surfaces. Programmers often choose Bézier surfaces for applications (such as an airplane cockpit simulator) that require real-time rendering.

problem.paragraph: Sometimes only one half of a Bézier curve needs further subdividing. For example, subdivision of the “left” side is accomplished with parts (a) and (c) of Exercise 17 and equation (8). When both halves of the curve $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ are divided, it is possible to organize calculations efficiently to calculate both left and right control points concurrently, without using equation (8) directly.

list.item: Show that the tangent vectors $$\textbf{y}^{\prime}(1)$$ and $$\textbf{z}^{\prime}(0)$$ are equal.

Using part (b) and the results of Exercises 17 and 18, write an algorithm that computes the control points for both $$\textbf{y}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{z}(t)$$ in an efficient manner. The only operations needed are sums and division by $$2$$ .

problem.paragraph: Explain why a cubic Bézier curve is completely determined by $$\textbf{x}(0)$$ , $$\mathbf{x}\prime(0)$$ , $$\textbf{x}(1)$$ , and $$\mathbf{x}\prime(1)$$ .﻿

TrueType® fonts, created by Apple Computer and Adobe Systems, use quadratic Bézier curves, while PostScript® fonts, created by Microsoft, use cubic Bézier curves. The cubic curves provide more flexibility for typeface design, but it is important to Microsoft that every typeface using quadratic curves can be transformed into one that uses cubic curves. Suppose that $$\textbf{w}(t)$$ is a quadratic curve, with control points $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ .﻿

list.item: Find control points $$\textbf{r}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{r}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{r}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{r}_{3}$$ such that the cubic Bézier curve $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ with these control points has the property that $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ and $$\textbf{w}(t)$$ have the same initial and terminal points and the same tangent vectors at $$t = 0$$ and $$t = 1$$ . (See Exercise 20.)
Show that if $$\textbf{x}(t)$$ is constructed as in part (a), then $$\textbf{x}(t) = \textbf{w}(t)$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 1$$ .﻿

problem.paragraph: Use partitioned matrix multiplication to compute the following matrix product, which appears in the alternative formula (5) for a Bézier curve: $$\left[\right. 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 - 3 & 3 & 0 & 0 3 & - 6 & 3 & 0 - 1 & 3 & - 3 & 1 \left]\right. \left[\right. p_{0} p_{1} p_{2} p_{3} \left]\right.$$

From equation (14) with $$t = 0$$ , $$\mathbf{x}(0) \neq \mathbf{p}_{0}$$ because $$\textbf{x} ( 0 ) = \frac{1}{6} [ \textbf{p}_{0} + 4 \textbf{p}_{1} + \textbf{p}_{2} ] = \frac{1}{6} \textbf{p}_{0} + \frac{2}{3} \textbf{p}_{1} + \frac{1}{6} \textbf{p}_{2} .$$

The coefficients are nonnegative and sum to $$1$$ , so $$\textbf{x}(0)$$ is in $$\text{conv\{} \textbf{p}_{0}, \textbf{p}_{1}, \textbf{p}_{2} \text{\}}$$ , and the affine coordinates with respect to $$\text{\{} \textbf{p}_{0}, \textbf{p}_{1}, \textbf{p}_{2} \text{\}}$$ are $$\left( {\frac{1}{6},\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{6}} \right)$$ .﻿

From equation (14) with $$t = 1$$ , $$\mathbf{x}(1) \neq \mathbf{p}_{3}$$ because $$\textbf{x} ( 1 ) = \frac{1}{6} [ \textbf{p}_{1} + 4 \textbf{p}_{2} + \textbf{p}_{3} ] = \frac{1}{6} \textbf{p}_{1} + \frac{2}{3} \textbf{p}_{2} + \frac{1}{6} \textbf{p}_{3} .$$

The coefficients are nonnegative and sum to $$1$$ , so $$\textbf{x}(1)$$ is in $$\text{conv\{} \textbf{p}_{1}, \textbf{p}_{2}, \textbf{p}_{3} \text{\}}$$ , and the affine coordinates with respect to $$\text{\{} \textbf{p}_{1}, \textbf{p}_{2}, \textbf{p}_{3} \text{\}}$$ are $$\left( {\frac{1}{6},\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{6}} \right)$$ .﻿

section.paragraph: In Exercises 1–21, mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

list.item: (T/F) Given $$\textbf{v}_{1} ,$$ $$\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and scalars $$c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$$ , an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$$ is a linear combination $$c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{v}_{p}$$ such that the weights satisfy $$c_{1} + \cdots + c_{p} = 1$$ .﻿
(T/F) The affine hull of two points $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ is the set of all points $$\textbf{y} = t\textbf{v}_{1} + (1 - t)\textbf{v}_{2}$$ , with $$t$$ in $$\mathbb{R}$$ .﻿
(T/F) A hyperplane is a $$\text{4-dimensional}$$ flat.
(T/F) Two flats are parallel if their intersection is empty.
(T/F) Every subspace is a flat.
(T/F) Every subspace is an affine set.
(T/F) Every affinely dependent set is linearly dependent.
(T/F) Every affinely independent set is linearly independent.
(T/F) The barycentric coordinates of a point in $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ are always nonnegative.

(T/F) Let $$S = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$$ be an affinely independent set in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Then each point $$\textbf{p}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ has a unique representation as an affine combination of $$\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}$$ .﻿

(T/F) A convex combination of points $$\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ is a linear combination of the form $$c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2} + \cdots + c_{k}\textbf{v}_{k}$$ such that $$c_{1} + c_{2} + \cdots + c_{k} = 1$$ and $$c_{i} \geq 0$$ for all $$i$$ .﻿

(T/F) If a set $$S$$ is affinely independent and if $$\textbf{p} \in \text{aff} S$$ , then $$\textbf{p} \in \text{conv} S$$ if and only if the barycentric coordinates of $$\textbf{p}$$ with respect to $$S$$ are nonnegative.
(T/F) The line segment between $$\textbf{x}$$ and $$\textbf{y}$$ is the set of all points of the form $$(1 - t)\textbf{x} + t\textbf{y}$$ , where $$t$$ is in $$\mathbb{R}$$ .﻿
(T/F) Every affine set is a convex set.
(T/F) For some $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the dimension of a hyperplane can be the same as the dimension of a line.
(T/F) For some $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the dimension of a hyperplane can be less than the dimension of a line.
(T/F) Suppose $$A$$ and $$B$$ are nonempty compact convex sets. Then there exists a hyperplane that strictly separates $$A$$ and $$B$$ if and only if $$A \cap B = \varnothing$$ .﻿
(T/F) A polytope can be the convex hull of infinitely many points.
(T/F) Every nonempty compact convex set $$S$$ has an extreme point, and the set of all extreme points is the smallest subset of $$S$$ whose convex hull is equal to $$S$$ .﻿

(T/F) If $$\textbf{w}(t)$$ is a quadratic Bézier curve with control points $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ , $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ , and $$\textbf{p}_{2}$$ , then $$\mathbf{w}\prime(0)$$ has the same direction as the tangent to the curve at $$\textbf{p}_{0}$$ and $$\mathbf{w}\prime(1)$$ has the same direction as the tangent to the curve at $$\textbf{p}_{1}$$ .﻿
(T/F) When two Bézier curves are connected with $$G^{1}$$ geometric continuity, then the tangent vectors for the two curves at the common control point have the same direction.
If $$S = \{\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{k}\}$$ is an affinely independent subset of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , prove that $$k \leq n + 1$$ .﻿
Suppose that $$F$$ and $$G$$ are $$k \text{-dimensional}$$ flats $$(0 \leq k \leq n - 1)$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ with $$F \subseteq G$$ . Prove that $$F = G$$ .﻿

Prove or give a counterexample: A set $$S$$ is convex if and only if for each $$\textbf{p}$$ , $$\textbf{q}$$ in $$S$$ , the set of points of the form $$(1 - t)\textbf{p} + t\textbf{q}$$ , where $$0 < t < 1$$ , is contained in $$S$$ .﻿

Let $$V$$ be a $$k \text{-dimensional}$$ subspace $$(0 \leq k \leq n - 1)$$ of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and let $$F_{1} = \textbf{x}_{1} + V$$ and $$F_{2} = \textbf{x}_{2} + V$$ for vectors $$\textbf{x}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{x}_{2}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Prove that either $$F_{1} = F_{2}$$ or $$F_{1} \cap F_{2} = \varnothing$$ . Thus two parallel flats either coincide or are disjoint.

Let $$f$$ be a nonzero linear functional on $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and suppose $$H = \lbrack f:7\rbrack$$ . If $$\textbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , $$f\left( \textbf{p} \right) = 2$$ , and $$H_{1} = H + 3\textbf{p}$$ , then find $$d$$ such that $$H_{1} = \lbrack f:d\rbrack$$ .﻿

Let $$V$$ be an $$(n - 1) \text{-dimensional}$$ subspace of $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ and suppose $$\textbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$$ but $$\textbf{p} \notin V$$ . Prove that each vector $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ has a unique representation as $$\textbf{x} = \textbf{v} + c\textbf{p}$$ , where $$\textbf{v} \in V$$ and $$c \in \mathbb{R}$$ .﻿

If $$m$$ is the maximum value of the linear functional $$f$$ on the convex set $$S$$ , and $$\textbf{p}$$ , $$\textbf{q}$$ are points in $$S$$ such that $$f\left( \textbf{p} \right) = f\left( \textbf{q} \right) = m$$ , show that $$f(\textbf{x}) = m$$ for all $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\overset{‾}{\textbf{pq}}$$ .﻿
